title: Infections of the Oral Cavity, Neck, and Head

questions.question: A man with an odontogenic infection is on amoxicillin with no improvement on therapy.
questions.question_raw: 18. A man with an odontogenic infection on amoxicillin. No improvement on therapy.

parts.text: Name two typical organisms that would not be covered by amoxicillin therapy alone.
Name two organisms that would not be covered by metronidazole alone.
Why does metronidazole only work for anaerobes?

parts_raw.text: Name 2 typical organisms that would not be covered by amoxicillin therapy alone
Name 2 organisms that would not be covered by metronidazole alone
Why does metronidazole only work for anaerobes.

questions.model_answer: a) Beta-lactamase-producing oral anaerobic gram-negative bacteria, which account for penicillin/amoxicillin failure: (1) pigmented Prevotella spp. (2) Fusobacterium spp. (Porphyromonas spp. also acceptable). b) Metronidazole has no aerobic/facultative activity, so it misses: (1) viridans (and other) streptococci (2) Actinomyces spp. c) Metronidazole is a prodrug requiring reductive activation: only obligate anaerobes possess the low-redox-potential electron-transport proteins (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase/ferredoxin) that reduce its nitro group to cytotoxic nitroso radicals, which then fragment bacterial DNA. Aerobes lack this reductive machinery (and oxygen re-oxidizes any activated drug), so the drug is never activated in them.
questions.beyond_mandell: Metronidazole's reductive-activation mechanism is not stated in this chapter; it is standard antimicrobial pharmacology (Mandell antibacterial-agents chapters).

parts.text: Name two bugs not covered by amoxicillin.
Name two bugs not covered by metronidazole.
Explain why metronidazole covers anaerobes and not aerobes.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 bugs not covered by amox
Name 2 bugs not covered by metronidazole
Explain why metronidazole only covers anaerobe and not aerobe

questions.model_answer: a) Beta-lactamase-producing oral anaerobic gram-negative rods: (1) pigmented Prevotella spp. (2) Fusobacterium spp. (Porphyromonas spp. also acceptable). b) Aerobes/facultatives, which lie outside metronidazole's spectrum: (1) viridans streptococci (2) Actinomyces spp. c) Metronidazole must be reductively activated by low-redox electron carriers (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase/ferredoxin) found only in anaerobes; the reduced nitro radical breaks bacterial DNA strands. Aerobes lack these carriers and oxygen re-oxidizes the intermediate, so the drug is never activated.
questions.beyond_mandell: Reductive-activation mechanism is standard pharmacology, not given in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Bugs not covered by amox: Fusobacterium (some resistance to PCN, significant resistance to clindamycin and linezolid; susceptible to Flagyl, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos and carbapenems); Prevotella (significant resistance to clindamycin; susceptible to Flagyl, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos, carbapenems, linezolid); Porphyromonas (susceptible to Flagyl and beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos, carbapenems, linezolid; significant resistance to clindamycin); Peptostreptococcus. Bugs not covered by metronidazole: all the aerobes - Streptococcus, Moraxella, Lactobacillus, Enterobacteriaceae. Why metronidazole only covers anaerobes: the enzyme that activates/oxidizes metronidazole (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase / ferredoxin) is only present in anaerobic bacteria, not aerobic ones.

questions.question: A young girl develops upper respiratory tract infection symptoms followed by neck swelling, trismus, and torticollis with no adenopathy noted; she looks toxic.
questions.question_raw: Young girl with URTI sx followed by neck swelling, trismus, torticollis, no adenopathy noted. Looks toxic.

parts.text: Give the most likely diagnosis and differential diagnosis.

parts_raw.text: A) Give most likely diagnosis and ddx

questions.model_answer: a) Most likely diagnosis: retropharyngeal abscess/space infection (post-URTI child with trismus, torticollis, toxic appearance, bulging posterior pharyngeal wall). DDx: (1) lateral pharyngeal (parapharyngeal) space infection (2) peritonsillar abscess (3) epiglottitis/bacterial tracheitis (4) cervical/retropharyngeal adenitis or suppurative lymphadenitis (5) meningitis. b) (1) Secure/monitor the airway (early intubation or tracheostomy if threatened). (2) High-dose IV empirical antibiotics covering streptococci, oral anaerobes and URTI pathogens (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) - ampicillin-sulbactam (or ceftriaxone) plus metronidazole, or clindamycin; add vancomycin if MRSA suspected. (3) Prompt ENT surgical drainage of loculated pus. c) (1) Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck to confirm, localize and define extent of abscess (mediastinal spread). (2) Lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph showing retropharyngeal widening. (3) CBC, electrolytes, creatinine and blood cultures. (4) Gram stain and aerobic/anaerobic culture of drained pus; throat swab for group A streptococcus.

cohort_answer.text:
Retropharyngeal abscess. DDx: Bacterial epiglottitis, peritonsillar abscess, croup, bacterial tracheitis, diphtheria, angioedema, foreign body, uvulitis, Ludwig angina
Airway management +/- ventilation; CTX +/- Vancomycin if resistant gram positives; +/- Flagyl for abscess. Most common organisms: S. aureus, GAS, S. pneumo, H flu, N meningitidis. Secure airway, consult ENT for drainage, start Abx (amp-sulbactam or clinda, or CTX+flagyl+/-vanco depending on local MRSA rates)
BW (CBC, lytes, Cr); BCx; throat swab for GAS if possible; imaging (lateral xrays of neck); micro from drainage if possible

questions.model_answer: a) Aerobic/facultative organisms outside metronidazole's spectrum: (1) viridans streptococci (2) Actinomyces spp. b) Beta-lactamase-producing oral anaerobic gram-negative rods: (1) pigmented Prevotella spp. (2) Fusobacterium spp. (Porphyromonas spp. also acceptable). c) Metronidazole requires reductive activation by low-redox electron-transport proteins (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase/ferredoxin) found only in anaerobic bacteria; once reduced, the nitro radical fragments DNA. Aerobes lack this reductive machinery and ambient oxygen re-oxidizes any activated drug, so it is never converted to its cytotoxic form.
questions.beyond_mandell: Reductive-activation mechanism is standard pharmacology, not stated in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: a) Actinomyces; Propionibacterium acnes; Lactobacillus. b) H. flu (beta lactamase); Moraxella (beta lactamase); B. fragilis; Prevotella. c) Reductive activation only occurs in obligate anaerobes; reductive particles (nitrogen radicals) interact with DNA causing strand breakage and fatal destabilization of DNA helix.
